# B2B2C Reseller Support

`customer_support.model.b2b2c_reseller_support` · model · parent `—`

> Our customer is another support organisation. Every contact arrives from a trained professional who has already run tier one, consulted their own runbook, and failed — which means the easy contacts structurally never reach us. Our queue is, by construction, somebody else's escalation tail: tiny in volume, brutal in average difficulty, and completely unbenchmarkable against a direct queue. A leader who imports handle-time or first-contact- resolution targets from a consumer operation will conclude within a month that this is the worst-performing team in the company, and will be measuring the wrong population. . The second structural fact is that all evidence is hearsay. We cannot see the end customer's screen, cannot ask them a follow-up, and cannot reproduce anything without a proxy. A question we would answer in ninety seconds on a live chat becomes a two-day round trip through two queues, and each hop loses fidelity — the reseller's agent paraphrases the customer, we paraphrase the agent, and the fault we finally investigate is three descriptions removed from the fault that exists. Reproduction stops being a step inside diagnosis and becomes the branch's hardest discipline: getting the right evidence requested, in the right words, in one round trip, because a second round trip costs another day of somebody else's SLA. . Third: there are two clocks and only one of them is ours. The reseller promised their customer four hours, has spent three of them, and reaches us with one hour left — and presents that as urgency rather than as contract, because it is not our contract. Our clock starts when they report, which is late by definition; theirs started when the customer complained. That gap is the source of nearly every escalation in this branch, and it is a structural mismatch rather than a service failure. It cannot be fixed by responding faster; it can only be managed by making the two clocks explicit to both sides. . Fourth: our words are republished by somebody with a commercial reason to soften them. What we write is forwarded, paraphrased, or pasted into the reseller's own template — and the caveats go first. "We believe this is fixed in the next release, subject to testing" reaches the end customer as "it is fixed next release". The correct craft here is to write for republication: short, quotable, self-contained statements that survive being cut, with the conditional part structurally inseparable from the claim. . Fifth: a substantial share of escalations are evidentiary rather than technical. The reseller needs something in writing to show their customer — a position, a date, an acknowledgement — and escalating to us is how they get it. Reading those as demands for more engineers produces the wrong response entirely. What is needed is a written, quotable, dated position, and it can usually be produced in an hour by someone who understands what is being asked for. . What an operator carries over wrongly from direct B2B: treating the requester's emotional state as the customer's. The reseller's agent is either professionally calm about a situation that is on fire, or escalated about something minor because their own manager is escalated. Neither register maps to the end user's actual state, and both mislead. The second carry-over error is closing the ticket when the reseller's agent understands the answer. Their understanding is not the resolution — the resolution is their customer's problem stopping, and we will never see it happen. Anything we learn about whether it worked comes back only as a re-open, weeks later, through the same two queues.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | a support agent or technical lead employed by the reseller, working to their own SLA, describing a problem they have not personally experienced on a system they do not own |
| typical_resolution_hours | 24 |
| volume_shape | very low ticket count against very high difficulty; volume is driven by the reseller's own book and spikes in correlated bursts when one of their platforms or campaigns breaks |
| staffing_model | a small senior partner-facing team with fast engineering access, plus a named partner manager per reseller |
| coverage | aligned to the reseller's commitments to their own customers, which are usually wider than anything we sell directly and were agreed without us |
| automation_level | low on contacts, high on enablement — deflection here means the reseller's agent finding the answer in partner documentation, which is a professional-audience content product and not a help centre |
| primary_channels | `ticket_portal`, `email`, `chat`, `phone` |
| notes | Concentration risk has no analogue in a direct branch. Losing one reseller is not losing a customer, it is losing their entire book at once, and the decision is taken by a partner manager who reads our support performance as a supplier-scorecard line. This is the only branch where a single unresolved ticket can plausibly be a material commercial event, and it is also the branch where the smallest number of people at the customer see our work.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.requester`

Requires `reports_on_behalf_of`, `role_title`, `technical_fluency`


> `reports_on_behalf_of` is an edge case in the canonical object and is populated on every single ticket here — it is the branch in one attribute. It also carries a second-order reading worth having: a reseller agent who consistently reports on behalf of the same end customer is dealing with a recurring fault their own tier one cannot hold, which is an enablement gap on our side long before it is a defect on ours.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `external_ref`, `account_ref`, `requester_ref`


> The reseller's own ticket id is the only join key between our record and the problem as it actually exists. Without it, neither party can reconcile a list of open issues, every status meeting is spent matching descriptions to descriptions, and a customer-affecting fault can be closed on our side while open on theirs with nobody able to prove it. Nothing else in this branch is as cheap to fix or as consistently skipped.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.sla_target`

Requires `started_at`, `measured_from`, `target_at`


> Our clock and theirs are different clocks and ours starts later. `measured_from` has to record which event started it — their customer's complaint or their report to us — because the whole of this branch's escalation pressure lives in the difference, and a target that looks comfortably met against our clock can be two hours past breach against the one the end customer is experiencing.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.entitlement`

Requires `plan`, `named_contacts`, `entitled_channels`


> Entitlement stops at the reseller. The end customer holds nothing from us at all, which means any promise made to them was made by someone with no authority to make it — and it will still be quoted at us. The practical control is the named contact list: contacts outside it are usually the reseller's own escalations routing around their tier one, which is worth noticing because it is the earliest sign that their support organisation is failing and their volume is about to become ours.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.knowledge_article`

Requires `audience`, `article_type`, `accuracy_state`


> Partner documentation is a different product from customer documentation, written for a trained professional who wants the mechanism rather than the reassurance. Publishing the consumer article to partners is the standard mistake and it insults the reader; publishing the partner article to consumers leaks internals. `audience` is what keeps them apart, and conflating them is how the enablement lever quietly stops working.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.escalation`

Requires `origin`, `reason`, `reason_note`


> Separate the evidentiary escalation from the technical one — the reseller frequently needs a written, dated position to show their own customer, not more capacity on the problem. `reason_note` is where that distinction survives, and getting it right converts a three-day engineering interrupt into an hour of careful writing.

> satisfaction_measurement is deliberately kept rather than deactivated, with the measured party overridden. It runs, and it measures how usable we are to a trained intermediary — a real and useful thing — while telling us nothing about the market whose experience we determine. Naming that blind spot in the override is more honest than deleting the capability and pretending the survey was never sent.
